The database tool (dbtool.html) opens SQLite database files and connects to PostgreSQL servers: browse the schema, write and run SQL, view and edit table data, export results.

SQLite databases

  • New SQLite creates an empty database, Open SQLite… (Ctrl+O) opens a database file (.sqlite, .db, …); you can also drop the file onto the window. Several databases can be open at the same time (list Open databases on the left).
  • The database is edited in memory. Save database (Ctrl+S) writes it back: directly into the file in Chrome/Edge on the desktop, as a download in Firefox and on Android (replace the original file with it). Changed databases are marked with •.

SQLite works completely offline.

PostgreSQL servers

A Postgres server is reached through the local relay (see the user guide, "Network functions and the relay").

  1. Connect to Postgres… opens the connection dialog: name, host, port (5432), database, user, password, SSL (prefer, require, disable; optionally accept self-signed certificates) and the relay address and token. Test checks the relay.
  2. Connect opens the connection; Save connection adds it to Saved connections (the password only if you tick the box).
  3. A click on a saved connection connects (or asks for the password if it was not saved); ✎ edits and × deletes a connection.

Password, MD5 and SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication are supported.

Saving connections

Saved connections and the relay settings are kept in a connections file. Save in the "Connections" area asks for the format:

  • KeePass database (encrypted with a password; recommended) — every connection becomes a KeePass entry in the group "Portable Web App Suite/dbtool" and can also be seen in KeePass;
  • JSON file (not encrypted; passwords would be readable).

Open… opens such a file again (KeePass asks for the password). The same file can hold the connections of the other suite applications.

Schema and SQL

  • Schema lists the tables (▦) and views (👁) of the active database; unfold a table to see its columns (🔑 = primary key, types, NOT NULL). ⟳ reloads the schema; it is reloaded automatically after CREATE, ALTER and DROP.
  • The SQL editor highlights SQL and completes keywords, table and column names (Ctrl+Space).
  • Run (Ctrl+Enter) runs the selected text, or the statement at the cursor; Run all (Ctrl+Shift+Enter) runs all statements.
  • Every statement with a result gets a result tab. The message line shows the number of changed rows, the duration or the error (for Postgres with SQL state code, detail and hint).
  • CSV and JSON export the shown result.
  • ⛁ ER diagram (above the schema) draws the tables and views with their columns (🔑 primary key, → foreign key) and the foreign-key relations, and opens the drawing in the diagram editor (referenced tables above the referencing ones), where it can be arranged, edited, printed or exported.
  • Explain shows how the database runs the current statement: for SQLite the query plan as a tree (SCAN = reads the whole table, SEARCH … USING INDEX = uses an index), for Postgres the text of EXPLAIN.
  • History in the side bar lists the last statements you ran (failed ones are underlined). A click puts a statement back into the editor, a double-click runs it again. The history is kept only in this browser; × deletes it.

Browsing and editing tables

Browse next to a table shows its rows (200 per page, ‹ and › page).

  • Double-click a cell to edit it; Enter saves, Escape cancels, Ctrl+Delete sets the value to NULL.
  • Add row opens a form with a field per column (empty fields use the column's default).
  • × deletes a row (after a confirmation).

Editing needs a primary key (SQLite tables without one are edited by their rowid). Every change is executed immediately as an UPDATE, INSERT or DELETE statement, which is shown in the message line.

Undo (↶, Ctrl+Z outside the SQL editor) and redo (↷, Ctrl+Y): in SQLite databases for every change, also by executed SQL statements (up to 20 steps, for databases up to 32 MiB); on PostgreSQL servers for the changes made in the result table (changed cells, deleted rows). The table is reloaded after undoing.

Keyboard shortcuts

On a Mac, use Cmd instead of Ctrl. F1 (or ?) shows this list in the application.

Ctrl+S Save the SQLite file
